cards.explanation: The answer is servants of Christ. Paul says men ought to regard him and Apollos, another teacher, as “…servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.” Notice what's missing: no throne, no trophy, no team jersey. A servant works for somebody else, friends, and Paul wants that to be the picture.

The word is faithful. Paul says, “Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” Look at what he asks for, friends. He doesn't ask for talent or a big following, just faithful. I like that, because anybody can do faithful, even a worn-out stamper.

The answer is True. Paul says, “In fact, I do not even judge myself.” He's already said he cares very little about being judged by the Corinthians or by any human court. So he's not holding a clipboard over himself either. I can barely take a bite of my own cookies without grading the corners.

The answer is the Lord. Paul says, “My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.” So even a clear conscience doesn't get the final say, friends. The Lord does.

The answer is the motives of men's hearts. Paul says the Lord “…will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts.” So it's not only what people did, but why. That's a good reason to hold off on judging, since we only see part of it.
The answer is False. Paul says, “At that time each will receive his praise from God.” It doesn't come from the church, friends. Nobody has to campaign for votes in that moment.

The answer is not to go beyond what is written. Paul says he applied these things to himself and Apollos so “…that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written.” Then, he says, they won't take pride in one man over another. Sounds like a good reason to keep our noses in the Book, bakers.

The word is pride. Paul says, “Then you will not take pride in one man over another.” That's the fan club problem in one sentence, friends. Learn not to go beyond what is written, and nobody needs to brag about their favorite teacher.

His point is that everything they have was given to them. Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” Then he asks, “And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” Everything the Corinthians have came to them as a gift, friends, so boasting as though it didn't doesn't fit.

The answer is False. Paul asks, “And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” He's questioning boasting as though what they have was never received. I've learned to say "thank you" before "look at me."

Paul's wish is that they really were kings. He says, “How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!” Just before it, he says, “Without us, you have become kings.” And if it were really true, friends, he'd get to be a king right alongside them.
The answer is False. Paul says the apostles have become “…a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.” So the audience isn't just men, friends. Angels are watching too.

The word is strong. Paul says, “We are weak, but you are strong.” He's lining the apostles up next to the Corinthians, and that's how the comparison goes. It's a hard line to read, bakers, but that's the word.
The apostles bless. Paul says, “When we are vilified, we bless…” When somebody insults you, blessing them back is a tough move, friends. I think I would've needed a minute in the pantry first.
The answer is True. Paul says, “…when we are slandered, we answer gently.” Somebody spreads a lie about you, and you answer gently. That takes a lot of strength, friends.

Paul writes to warn them as his beloved children. He says, “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.” It's a warning, and it comes with love. He's talking like a father, friends.

The word is imitate. Paul says, “Therefore I urge you to imitate me.” He's just told the Corinthians he became their father in Christ Jesus through the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15). So he asks them, as their father, to follow his example.

Timothy will remind them of Paul's way of life. Paul says Timothy “…will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.” So Timothy brings a reminder of how Paul lives, friends. It matches what Paul teaches everywhere.

The answer is True. Paul says, “But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing…” He's sending Timothy, and he plans to come himself, if the Lord is willing. Just before that he says, “Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you.” (1 Corinthians 4:18)

He'll find out what power they have. Paul says he will find out “…not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.” Talking is easy, friends. He wants to see what's behind it.

The answer is False. Paul says, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.” That fits what he just said about finding out what power the arrogant people have. Plenty of folks can talk, bakers. Power is what he wants to see.
